questions.title: Chemical that initiates the extrinsic phase of clotting
questions.question: Which chemical initiates the extrinsic phase of clotting?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fibrin is the end product of the cascade, formed from fibrinogen by thrombin, not the substance that starts the extrinsic pathway.
explanations.B: Correct. Tissue thromboplastin (tissue factor, factor III), released from damaged tissue at the site of vessel injury, is what triggers the extrinsic coagulation pathway. It activates factor X to factor Xa, which then converts prothrombin to thrombin, setting the whole cascade in motion from outside the blood itself — hence "extrinsic".
explanations.C: Incorrect. Prothrombin is converted into thrombin further down the cascade; it does not itself initiate the extrinsic pathway.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Christmas factor (factor IX) is a component of the intrinsic pathway, not the extrinsic pathway's trigger.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Fibrinogen is the precursor of fibrin, converted late in the cascade by thrombin; it plays no role in initiating the extrinsic pathway.

questions.learning_objective: Identify tissue thromboplastin as the trigger of the extrinsic coagulation pathway.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.116

questions.title: Factor that activates conversion of prothrombin to thrombin
questions.question: Which factor activates the conversion of prothrombin to thrombin?

explanations.A: Correct. Factor Xa is the activated clotting factor that directly converts prothrombin into active thrombin, the step common to both the extrinsic and intrinsic pathways once they converge. This conversion also requires calcium ions and phospholipid as cofactors, forming the prothrombinase complex.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Factor III (tissue thromboplastin) triggers the extrinsic pathway further upstream, activating factor X rather than directly converting prothrombin itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Factor VIII is a cofactor in the intrinsic pathway that accelerates factor X activation; it does not itself convert prothrombin to thrombin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Factor IXa acts upstream in the intrinsic pathway, together with factor VIIIa, to activate factor X — a step before prothrombin conversion, not the conversion itself.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Factor XIa acts further upstream still in the intrinsic pathway, activating factor IX; it is two steps removed from prothrombin conversion.

questions.learning_objective: Identify factor Xa as the clotting factor that directly converts prothrombin to thrombin.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.117

questions.title: Ion required for conversion of prothrombin into active thrombin
questions.question: Which of the following ions is required for conversion of prothrombin into active thrombin?

explanations.A: Correct. Calcium ions (Ca++) are required as a cofactor for the conversion of prothrombin into active thrombin by factor Xa. They are also needed more broadly at multiple other steps of the coagulation cascade, so the cascade cannot proceed without calcium even when every clotting factor is present. This is why citrate (a calcium chelator) is used as an anticoagulant to prevent stored blood from clotting.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ferrous iron (Fe++) is central to haemoglobin's oxygen-binding function, not a coagulation cofactor.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Magnesium ions participate in many enzymatic reactions in the body but are not the specific cofactor required for prothrombin-to-thrombin conversion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Manganese ions are not the coagulation cascade's required cofactor for this step.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Chloride is the major extracellular anion involved in osmotic and acid-base balance, not a coagulation cofactor.

questions.learning_objective: Identify calcium ions as a required cofactor for prothrombin-to-thrombin conversion.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.118

questions.title: Conversion of fibrinogen into fibrin is promoted by
questions.question: The conversion of fibrinogen into fibrin promoted by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Factor X (as factor Xa) acts upstream, converting prothrombin to thrombin, not fibrinogen to fibrin directly.
explanations.B: Correct. Thrombin, generated from prothrombin by factor Xa, is the enzyme that converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin strands. This fibrin meshwork stabilises the platelet plug into a definitive clot, and thrombin also activates factor XIII, which cross-links the fibrin strands to further strengthen the clot.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Prothrombin is the inactive precursor of thrombin itself, not the enzyme that acts on fibrinogen.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Platelets form the initial platelet plug and provide a surface for the cascade to occur on, but they do not enzymatically convert fibrinogen to fibrin.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Factor IX acts far upstream in the intrinsic pathway, activating factor X together with factor VIIIa; it does not act directly on fibrinogen.

questions.learning_objective: Identify thrombin as the enzyme that converts fibrinogen to fibrin.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.118

questions.title: Hereditary deficiency of coagulation
questions.question: A condition of heredity deficiency of coagulation is called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Anaemia is a reduction in red cell mass or haemoglobin, unrelated to a coagulation factor deficiency.
explanations.B: Correct. Haemophilia is the general name for a hereditary (inherited) deficiency of a specific coagulation factor, producing a lifelong bleeding tendency from otherwise minor injury or spontaneously into joints and soft tissue. Both major forms — haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) and haemophilia B (factor IX deficiency, Christmas disease) — are X-linked recessive, which is why haemophilia overwhelmingly affects males.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Haemolysis is the destruction of red blood cells, an unrelated process to a coagulation-factor deficiency.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Leukaemia is malignant, uncontrolled white cell proliferation, not a hereditary coagulation-factor deficiency.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Polycythemia is an increased red cell count, unrelated to coagulation-factor deficiency.

questions.learning_objective: Define haemophilia as a hereditary coagulation-factor deficiency.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.117

questions.title: Factor deficient in Hemophilia
questions.question: A deficiency of which of the following factors causes Hemophilia?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Factor III (tissue thromboplastin) triggers the extrinsic pathway; its deficiency is not what defines haemophilia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Factor V deficiency (parahaemophilia) is a distinct, much rarer bleeding disorder, not the classic haemophilia this question asks about.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Factor VII deficiency is a separate, rare bleeding disorder affecting the extrinsic pathway, not classic haemophilia.
explanations.D: Correct. Factor VIII deficiency is the cause of haemophilia A, the classic and most common form of haemophilia, an X-linked recessive condition producing a lifelong bleeding tendency. Factor VIII normally acts as a cofactor accelerating factor X activation in the intrinsic pathway, so its absence markedly slows clot formation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Factor X deficiency is a separate, rare bleeding disorder affecting the common pathway, not classic haemophilia.

questions.learning_objective: Identify factor VIII deficiency as the cause of the classic form of haemophilia (haemophilia A).

questions.title: Chemical that produces vasoconstriction of an injured blood vessel
questions.question: Which chemical produces vasoconstriction of injured blood vessel?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fibrin stabilising factor (factor XIII) cross-links fibrin strands to strengthen the clot; it has no vasoconstrictor action.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Plasmin degrades fibrin during fibrinolysis, the clot-breakdown process, and plays no role in vasoconstriction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Platelet factor 3 (platelet phospholipid) provides a surface for coagulation-factor assembly, not a vasoconstrictor action.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Stuart-Prower factor (factor X) is a coagulation-cascade enzyme precursor, not a vasoconstrictor.
explanations.E: Correct. Thromboxane A2, released from activated platelets, is a potent vasoconstrictor that narrows the injured vessel to reduce blood flow and blood loss while the platelet plug and coagulation cascade complete the job. It also promotes further platelet aggregation, which is why aspirin's inhibition of its synthesis both prolongs bleeding time and reduces vasoconstriction.

questions.learning_objective: Identify thromboxane A2 as the mediator of vasoconstriction at an injured vessel.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.118

questions.title: Factor that potentiates platelet adhesion
questions.question: Which factor potentiates (increases) platelet adhesion?

explanations.A: Incorrect. ADP, released from activated platelets, recruits and activates further platelets to reinforce aggregation, but it is not the molecule that potentiates the initial adhesion step to collagen.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Fibrin stabilising factor (factor XIII) cross-links fibrin after the clot has begun to form; it does not potentiate platelet adhesion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Thromboxane A2 causes vasoconstriction and promotes further aggregation, but it is not the molecule that bridges platelets to collagen at the adhesion step.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Tissue factor triggers the extrinsic coagulation cascade; it does not act on platelet adhesion.
explanations.E: Correct. Von Willebrand factor, a plasma glycoprotein, potentiates platelet adhesion to exposed subendothelial collagen at an injury site by bridging platelet surface receptors (glycoprotein Ib) to the collagen. Its deficiency (von Willebrand disease) is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, causing impaired primary haemostasis.

questions.learning_objective: Identify von Willebrand factor as the molecule that potentiates platelet adhesion to the injured vessel wall.

questions.title: Correct order of the steps of hemostasis
questions.question: Choose the correct order for the steps of hemostasis:

options.A: Blood coagulation, platelet plug formation, blood vessel spasm
options.B: Platelets plug formation, blood coagulation, blood vessel spasm
options.C: Blood vessel spasm, platelet plug formation, blood coagulation
options.D: Blood vessel spasm, blood coagulation, platelet plug formation
options.E: Platelet plug formation, blood vessel spasm, blood coagulation

explanations.A: Incorrect. This reverses the true order; blood vessel spasm is the fastest, most immediate response and comes first, not last.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This places blood vessel spasm last, when it is actually the immediate, first response to injury.
explanations.C: Correct. Normal haemostasis follows a fixed sequence: blood vessel spasm (vasoconstriction) narrows the injured vessel first to reduce flow; platelet plug formation then seals the breach as platelets adhere, activate and aggregate; blood coagulation follows, laying down fibrin that stabilises the platelet plug into a definitive clot. Each step builds on the one before it, and vessel spasm's speed (occurring within seconds) is what buys time for the slower platelet and coagulation responses to develop.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This places platelet plug formation after coagulation, when platelets actually form the initial plug that the coagulation cascade then stabilises.
explanations.E: Incorrect. This places vessel spasm after the platelet plug, when vessel spasm is actually the fastest, first response.

questions.learning_objective: State the correct order of the three haemostasis steps: vessel spasm, platelet plug formation, then coagulation.

questions.title: Substance released by activated platelets
questions.question: Activated platelets release which of the following:

explanations.A: Incorrect as the tested answer here. Serotonin is also released by activated platelets and contributes to vasoconstriction, but the department's own printed key for this item names ADP, testing recruitment/aggregation signalling specifically rather than the vasoactive amine.
explanations.B: Correct. Activated platelets release ADP from their dense granules, which recruits and activates further circulating platelets, reinforcing the aggregating platelet plug at the injury site. This positive-feedback recruitment is part of why an initially small platelet plug can rapidly grow to seal a breach.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Thromboplastin (tissue factor) is released from damaged tissue, not from platelets themselves.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Fibrin is the product of thrombin acting on fibrinogen in plasma, not a substance stored in and released by platelets.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Von Willebrand factor is a plasma glycoprotein (also stored in endothelial cells and platelet alpha granules) that potentiates platelet adhesion, but it is not the specific platelet-release product tested by this item.

questions.learning_objective: Identify ADP as a substance activated platelets release to recruit further platelets.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.120

questions.title: Cells necessary for clot retraction
questions.question: ------------- are necessary for clot retraction to occur.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Red blood cells are passively trapped within the fibrin meshwork of a clot but play no active contractile role in clot retraction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lymphocytes mediate adaptive immunity and have no role in the mechanical process of clot retraction.
explanations.C: Correct. Platelets are necessary for clot retraction: after the fibrin clot has formed, the platelet cytoskeleton contracts, pulling the fibrin meshwork tighter and squeezing out serum. This draws the wound edges together and makes the clot more effective at sealing the vessel, and clot retraction is impaired in conditions of severe thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Basophils mediate immediate hypersensitivity reactions and have no role in clot retraction.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Monocytes are phagocytic precursor cells with no contractile role in clot retraction.

questions.learning_objective: Identify platelets as necessary for clot retraction after fibrin clot formation.

questions.title: Vitamin K dependent coagulation factors
questions.question: Vitamin K dependent coagulation factors are:

options.A: Factor II, VII, IX and X

explanations.A: Correct. Factors II (prothrombin), VII, IX and X, along with proteins C and S, require vitamin K for their hepatic synthesis — vitamin K is a cofactor for the enzyme that carboxylates specific glutamate residues on these factors, activating them for calcium binding. Vitamin K deficiency (or vitamin K antagonists such as warfarin) lowers the functional level of all four factors together, prolonging coagulation time.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Factors XII and XI are contact-activation factors of the intrinsic pathway, and their synthesis is not vitamin K dependent.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Factors VIII and XI are also not vitamin K dependent; factor VIII in particular is synthesised independently of vitamin K status.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Factor III (tissue thromboplastin) and factors VIII and XI are not among the vitamin-K-dependent factors.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Factors XI and XII are contact-activation factors, not part of the vitamin-K-dependent group.

questions.learning_objective: Name factors II, VII, IX and X as the vitamin-K-dependent coagulation factors.

questions.title: Cause of hemorrhagic tendency in obstructive jaundice
questions.question: Hemorrhagic tendency in obstructive jaundice is due to:

options.D: Lack of factors II, VII, IX and X

explanations.A: Incorrect. Obstructive jaundice's bleeding tendency is not primarily from a platelet deficiency; platelet counts are typically normal.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Increased serum bile salts cause pruritus (itching) in obstructive jaundice, not the bleeding tendency, which has a separate mechanism.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Factor VIII synthesis is not vitamin K dependent and is not the mechanism behind obstructive jaundice's bleeding tendency.
explanations.D: Correct. In obstructive jaundice, blocked bile flow into the intestine prevents normal fat (and fat-soluble vitamin) absorption, including vitamin K, because bile salts are needed to emulsify and absorb it. The resulting vitamin K deficiency lowers hepatic synthesis of factors II, VII, IX and X, prolonging coagulation time and producing a hemorrhagic tendency — the same underlying factor group tested directly elsewhere in this cluster, here reached through a malabsorption mechanism rather than dietary deficiency alone.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Fibrinogen deficiency is not the mechanism of obstructive jaundice's bleeding tendency; fibrinogen synthesis is not vitamin K dependent.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that obstructive jaundice's hemorrhagic tendency comes from vitamin K malabsorption (via blocked bile flow) lowering factors II, VII, IX and X.
